text: Who is everywhere is nowhere.
author: Seneca the Younger
source: Letters to Lucilius, Letter II (c. 65), trans. Richard Mott Gummere; original Latin — https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Seneca_the_Younger#Letter_II:_On_discursiveness_in_reading

text: Lay hold of today's task, and you will not need to depend so much upon tomorrow's. While we are postponing, life speeds by.
author: Seneca the Younger
source: Letters to Lucilius, Letter I (c. 65), trans. Richard Mott Gummere; original Latin — https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Seneca_the_Younger#Letter_I:_On_Saving_Time

text: It is not that we have a short space of time, but that we waste much of it. Life is long enough.
author: Seneca the Younger
source: On the Shortness of Life, ch. 1 (c. 49), trans. John W. Basore; original Latin — https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Seneca_the_Younger

text: First say to yourself what you would be; and then do what you have to do.
author: Epictetus
source: Discourses III.23.1 (c. 108); original Greek — https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Epictetus

text: No thing great is created suddenly, any more than a bunch of grapes or a fig.
author: Epictetus
source: Discourses I.15.7 (c. 108); original Greek — https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Epictetus

text: A journey of a thousand li starts with a single step.
author: Laozi
source: Tao Te Ching, ch. 64; original Chinese — https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Laozi

text: He who has begun has half done. Dare to be wise; begin!
author: Horace
source: Epistles, Book I, epistle ii, lines 40–41 (c. 20 BC); original Latin — https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Horace

text: The beginning is the most important part of any work.
author: Plato
source: The Republic, 377a, trans. Benjamin Jowett; original Greek — https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Plato

text: Drops of water hollow out a stone.
author: Ovid
source: Epistulae ex Ponto IV.x.5 (c. AD 13), trans. Arthur Leslie Wheeler; original Latin — https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Ovid

text: If you should put even a little on a little, and should do this often, soon this too would become big.
author: Hesiod
source: Works and Days, lines 361–362 (c. 700 BC); original Greek — https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Hesiod

text: For the things we have to learn before we can do, we learn by doing.
author: Aristotle
source: Nicomachean Ethics, Book II, 1103a.33; original Greek — https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Aristotle

text: Learning without thought is labor lost; thought without learning is perilous.
author: Confucius
source: Analects, Book II, ch. XV, trans. James Legge (1861); original Chinese — https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Confucius

text: Practice is the best of all instructors.
author: Publilius Syrus
source: Sentences, maxim 439 (1st century BC), trans. Darius Lyman (1856); original Latin — https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Publilius_Syrus

text: If I have seen further it is by standing on ye sholders of Giants.
author: Isaac Newton
source: Letter to Robert Hooke, 5 February 1675/76 — https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Isaac_Newton

text: In the fields of observation chance favours only the prepared mind.
author: Louis Pasteur
source: Lecture, University of Lille, 7 December 1854; original French — https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Louis_Pasteur

text: Iron rusts from disuse; stagnant water loses its purity and in cold weather becomes frozen; even so does inaction sap the vigor of the mind.
author: Leonardo da Vinci
source: The Notebooks of Leonardo da Vinci, ed. Jean Paul Richter (1883), trans. R. C. Bell and E. J. Poynter; original Italian — https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Leonardo_da_Vinci

text: Genius is one percent inspiration, ninety-nine percent perspiration.
author: Thomas Edison
source: Letter, 1927, quoted in Argus Leader (21 February 1932) and Harper's Monthly (September 1932) — https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Thomas_Edison

text: Always bear in mind that your own resolution to succeed, is more important than any other one thing.
author: Abraham Lincoln
source: Letter to Isham Reavis, 5 November 1855 — https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Abraham_Lincoln

text: One never notices what has been done; one can only see what remains to be done.
author: Marie Curie
source: Letter to her brother, 1894; original French — https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Marie_Curie

text: Every noble work is at first impossible.
author: Thomas Carlyle
source: Past and Present (1843), Book III, ch. XI: Labour — https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Thomas_Carlyle

text: Few things are impossible to diligence and skill.
author: Samuel Johnson
source: The History of Rasselas, Prince of Abissinia (1759), ch. XII — https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Samuel_Johnson

text: Ever tried. Ever failed. No matter. Try again. Fail again. Fail better.
author: Samuel Beckett
source: Worstward Ho (1983) — https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Samuel_Beckett

text: Never give in — never, never, never, never, in nothing great or small, large or petty, never give in except to convictions of honour and good sense.
author: Winston Churchill
source: Speech at Harrow School, 29 October 1941 — https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Winston_Churchill

text: I have learned that success is to be measured not so much by the position that one has reached in life as by the obstacles which he has overcome while trying to succeed.
author: Booker T. Washington
source: Up From Slavery (1901), ch. II: Boyhood Days — https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Booker_T._Washington

text: I'm not afraid of storms, for I'm learning how to sail my ship.
author: Louisa May Alcott
source: Little Women (1868), ch. 44 (Amy) — https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Louisa_May_Alcott
